definition: A gas laser with a red beam, used in the first supermarket barcode scanners.
A sensor that turns light into an electrical signal; scanners and disc players use them to read reflections.
A tiny pressed mark on a CD, DVD or Blu-ray that reflects light differently from the flat surface, encoding bits.
The smallest spot a lens can focus light into, set by the wavelength.
How wide a cone of light a lens gathers. A higher value focuses a smaller spot; Blu-ray uses 0.85.
The spacing between neighboring turns of a disc's spiral track, about 320 nm on Blu-ray.
A stretch of fiber laced with erbium and pumped by a laser at 980 or 1480 nm, which boosts 1550 nm signals without turning them into electronics.
Wavelength division multiplexing: sending several closely spaced laser colors down one fiber to multiply capacity.
Light detection and ranging: measuring distance by timing laser pulses.
Distance equals half the round-trip time of a light pulse multiplied by the speed of light.
Vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, a tiny chip laser that emits from its surface, used in phone depth sensors.
A US court hearing on whether a scientific method is generally accepted before evidence from it is admitted.
An instrument that splits a laser beam down two arms and recombines it, so tiny changes in length show up as light. The core of LIGO.
The fractional change in length a gravitational wave causes; 10^-21 for the 2015 detection.
The centimeter-sized gold cylinder at NIF that turns laser light into x-rays to squeeze the fuel capsule.
A fusion shot that releases more energy than the laser energy delivered to the target.
Crossed pairs of laser beams that slow atoms as if they were moving through syrup.
A clock that holds atoms in a grid of laser light and probes them with a clock laser at an optical frequency.
A three-mirror prism that sends light straight back where it came from; Apollo 11's panel holds 100 of them.
An artificial star made by a laser exciting sodium atoms about 90 km up, used to correct telescope blur.
A deformable mirror that reshapes itself about 1000 times a second to cancel atmospheric blur.
Stretching a laser pulse, amplifying it, then recompressing it to reach extreme peak power.
10^15 watts of peak power, held for only femtoseconds.
A tightly focused laser that can hold and move tiny objects, including living cells.
